2026-07-11.intro: Today's throughline: the tech keeps getting easier, but the harder work is organizational — redesigning how teams operate, choosing tools that will still exist next quarter, and figuring out the new etiquette of talking about AI use out loud.

trends.title: The bottleneck isn't the AI anymore — it's your org chart
trends.body: Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index confirms what a lot of planners already suspect: handing people AI tools isn't the same as building an organization that can actually use them. Only 19% of AI users fall into the "Frontier" zone where individual skill and organizational readiness are both high — the rest are stuck, blocked, or still figuring it out (Microsoft Work Trend Index, May 2026). The tension is real: 65% of AI users fear falling behind if they don't adapt quickly, while 45% say it feels safer to just stick to their current workflow.

slants.strategy: Treat AI readiness as a structural project on your roadmap — audit where governance, incentives, and workflows still assume a pre-AI operating model, not just where headcount happens to use AI tools.
slants.operations: Map which processes have people using AI ad hoc versus which ones have actually been redesigned end-to-end around it — that gap is where inconsistency and rework hide.
slants.pm: Bake 'who reviews the AI's output and how' into project plans up front, instead of bolting it on after a rollout stalls.
slants.admin: If you've quietly gotten ahead of your team on AI, that's a signal worth surfacing — flag the gap between what you've figured out and what your team's official workflow supports.

steps: Pick one recurring task on your team that people already use AI for informally.

Ask your company-approved AI tool: "Here's a recurring task on my team: [describe task]. Write a simple three-step workflow showing where a human should review or approve the AI's output before it's used."
Compare that draft workflow to what actually happens today — is there a real review step, or does AI output go straight out the door?
Write down one gap between the ideal workflow and the current one.
Share your gap and the AI-drafted workflow in the group.

trends.title: AI tools are getting bought, buried, or both — plan around it
trends.body: The AI tools market just had its biggest shakeup yet: SpaceX's reported $60 billion acquisition of the coding tool Cursor was the largest startup acquisition ever recorded, part of a quarter where roughly 80% of venture investment went to AI startups (AI tools news roundup, July 2026). The steadier trend matters more for planners: 193 AI tools have already shut down or been acquired this year, and Cursor itself acquired a smaller rival just three weeks before being bought — proof that the tool your team builds a workflow around today may look totally different by next quarter.

slants.strategy: Build vendor-churn risk into your AI roadmap the way you'd plan for a key supplier being acquired — assume today's tool stack looks different in 12 months.
slants.operations: Before standardizing a process around any single AI tool, check whether your company-approved option has a stable enterprise agreement, not just a promising free tier.
slants.pm: Add a 'tool continuity' line to project risk logs for any initiative that leans heavily on one AI vendor.
slants.admin: If you've built a personal system around one free AI tool, keep a backup habit going with a second one — free tiers are shrinking fast across the board.

steps: List the AI tools you or your team currently rely on for any part of your workflow.

Ask your company-approved AI tool: "I rely on [tool name] for [task]. If this tool changed its pricing, got acquired, or shut down tomorrow, what's a backup approach using a different tool or a manual process?"
Review the answer and pick one backup you could realistically use.
Write the backup plan down in one sentence.
Share your primary tool and backup plan in the group.

trends.title: Being honest about using AI at work is quietly costing people
trends.body: New research from Atlassian's Teamwork Lab found something uncomfortable: even though 94% of knowledge workers use AI at work, disclosing it still carries a real penalty. In a controlled experiment, colleagues who admitted to using AI were rated 10x lazier and 24 points less likely to get recommended for a high-visibility project than peers who produced identical work without mentioning AI (Atlassian Teamwork Lab, June 2026). Framing your AI use as helping the team, rather than just saving yourself time, closed much of that gap.

slants.strategy: Set explicit team norms for how AI use gets discussed in planning documents and reviews — silence isn't a policy, it's a vacuum that culture will fill on its own.
slants.operations: Close the trust gap fastest by using AI visibly yourself and narrating it as a team efficiency win, not a personal shortcut.
slants.pm: Build 'AI-assisted' into status update templates as a normal field, so disclosing it stops feeling like a confession.
slants.admin: If you're already the AI power user on your team, you have a chance to model open, team-framed AI use before the culture defaults to secrecy.

steps: Think of one task you've used AI for recently but haven't mentioned to your manager or team.
Ask your company-approved AI tool: "Help me write a two-sentence note to my manager describing how I used AI to complete [task], framed around how it helped the team rather than just saving me time."
Read the draft and adjust it so it sounds like you.
Send it, or say it out loud in your next team check-in.
Share what you sent or said in the group.

homework.title: Let AI interview you before it plans your weekend
homework.body: Instead of dumping every trip detail into one giant prompt, try teaching the AI to ask you questions first — it's a technique that gets noticeably better results for any personal project, from trip planning to gift shopping. Use whichever free tool you like: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity.
homework.prompt: I want to plan a two-day weekend trip within driving distance. Before you suggest anything, ask me five questions about my budget, interests, and who's coming — then use my answers to give me three ranked options.

2026-07-12.intro: Sunday. A quieter day to catch up, reset, and prepare. This week's drop is lighter — one key development and a powerful use case to try at your own pace.

trends.title: AI Is Getting Dramatically Better at Understanding Your Documents
trends.body: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google all updated their document understanding capabilities this month, with significant improvements in table extraction, cross-reference understanding, and multi-page reasoning. The practical effect: you can now drop a 100-page PDF into Claude or GPT-4o and ask it sophisticated questions that require reading across multiple sections simultaneously. Legal teams piloting these updated capabilities reported cutting document review time for contracts, compliance documents, and regulatory filings by 65–75% (LexisNexis, July 2026).

slants.strategy: Better document understanding means your AI can now analyze lengthy RFPs, annual reports, and strategic plans with the same accuracy as a trained analyst — incorporate this into your competitive intelligence and planning cycles.
slants.operations: Contracts, SOPs, compliance docs, and audit reports are all candidates for AI-first review — if you're still reading long documents linearly before extracting key points, you're spending time you don't need to.
slants.pm: AI that reads across a 100-page requirements document or technical specification to surface inconsistencies, gaps, and dependencies is now available to every PM — use it on your next spec review.
slants.admin: Board packs, legal agreements, and policy documents that used to require hours of careful reading can now be summarized and queried in minutes — this is one of the highest-leverage applications for executive support.

steps: Find a long document you've been meaning to read but haven't — a report, a policy, a contract.
Upload it to your company-approved AI tool (or paste the text).
Ask three questions that would normally require reading the entire document to answer.
Then ask: "What are the 5 most important things I need to know from this document, and what questions should I be asking that I haven't thought to ask yet?"
Share which question the AI's answer surprised you most on.

trends.title: The 'Human in the Loop' Standard Is Evolving
trends.body: The AI governance conversation shifted this week as the IEEE published new guidelines on human-AI oversight that distinguish between different categories of decisions based on reversibility and impact — rather than applying a blanket 'human must review' standard. The framework categorizes AI decisions into three tiers: fully autonomous (routine, low-impact, easily reversible), supervised autonomous (significant but recoverable), and human-required (high-stakes, hard to reverse) (IEEE Standards Association, July 2026). This is the governance model most enterprises are expected to adopt over the next 18 months.

slants.strategy: A tiered AI oversight framework is more pragmatic than blanket human review requirements — build your AI governance policy around reversibility and impact, not just 'did AI touch this?'
slants.operations: Mapping your AI-assisted workflows to this three-tier framework clarifies where you can run fully autonomous and where you need a human checkpoint — it also protects you in audits and compliance reviews.
slants.pm: Product features that include AI decision-making now have a clearer governance framework to design against — build your AI feature specs around which tier each decision falls into.
slants.admin: Understanding the tiered governance model helps you advise executives on AI risk: routine AI-assisted tasks are different from high-stakes AI decisions, and conflating the two leads to either over-caution or under-caution.

steps: List three ways you currently use AI in your work.
For each one, classify it using the IEEE's three-tier model: fully autonomous, supervised autonomous, or human-required.

Open your company-approved AI tool: "Based on this framework [describe the tiers], help me assess whether my use of AI for [task] is appropriately supervised or whether I should adjust my level of oversight."
Identify one AI task you're over-supervising (wasting time) and one you might be under-supervising (taking on risk).
Share your classification and whether the framework changed how you think about AI oversight.

trends.title: Sunday Prompt: Let AI Help You Plan the Week Ahead
trends.body: One of the most practical uses of AI is weekly planning — not just listing tasks, but thinking through priorities, blockers, and what 'success' actually looks like. Sunday is the ideal time to build this habit, and it only takes 10 minutes with the right prompt.

slants.strategy: Strategic planning at the weekly level is a compounding habit — spending 10 minutes on Sunday with AI to structure your week pays dividends every day that follows.
slants.operations: Weekly AI-assisted planning helps you identify resource conflicts, dependencies, and low-priority tasks that might crowd out high-impact work before the week starts.
slants.pm: A weekly AI planning session helps PMs stay out ahead of blockers, stakeholder communication needs, and sprint dependencies — try it as a standing Sunday evening routine.
slants.admin: Executive support requires anticipating what's needed before it's asked for — AI-assisted weekly planning helps you get ahead of your executive's needs rather than reacting to them.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool on Sunday evening.
Share your top 5 priorities for the week and any known constraints or blockers.
Ask: "Help me plan this week so the most important things actually get done. Suggest a day-by-day structure that protects time for deep work and builds in buffer for surprises."
Review the suggested plan and adjust it to your reality.
Check back at the end of the week: share whether the plan held and what you'd do differently.

homework.title: Create your AI planning ritual
homework.body: The most effective AI users aren't using it reactively — they have a small set of rituals that keep them ahead. A Sunday planning session is one of the most powerful. Try structuring yours with this prompt and see if it becomes a habit.
homework.prompt: I want to start using AI for weekly planning. Help me build a 10-minute Sunday ritual. Start by asking me about my upcoming week — my priorities, my meetings, my constraints, and my energy level. Then help me build a plan that maximizes my impact and protects my focus time.

2026-07-13.intro: Monday. New week. Three AI developments from last week that set the tone for what's coming — and one habit to build into this week's work.

trends.title: Salesforce Einstein Gets a Major Upgrade — AI Is Now Running Sales Cycles
trends.body: Salesforce announced Einstein Autopilot last week — a suite of AI agents that can manage lead follow-up, schedule meetings, draft proposals, and update CRM records autonomously. The system runs on Salesforce Data Cloud, meaning it has full context of every customer interaction. Early adopters in the beta reported a 45% increase in pipeline conversion rates and a 60% reduction in CRM data entry time for sales teams (Salesforce, July 2026). The AI sales assistant is now actually autonomous — not just a helper.

slants.strategy: AI running sales cycle tasks autonomously means your sales team can focus entirely on relationship and judgment work — restructure compensation and success metrics for a world where AI handles execution.
slants.operations: The 60% reduction in CRM data entry time is the operations number to watch — any workflow downstream of CRM (reporting, forecasting, customer success) gets faster when the data is more accurate and complete.
slants.pm: AI-managed sales cycles generate richer data about what works and what doesn't in the funnel — build your product intelligence on top of this data by connecting it to feature requests and churn analysis.
slants.admin: Autonomous scheduling, proposal drafting, and follow-up mean the administrative layer of the sales cycle is handled — executive admins supporting sales leaders can now focus on more complex coordination and stakeholder management.

steps: Identify one step in your team's sales, client, or customer process that is repetitive and data-dependent — follow-up emails, status updates, or scheduling.
Open your company-approved AI tool and paste the context for one real pending task in that step.
Ask: "Draft an action for this step as if you were an autonomous AI agent: what would you do, what information would you gather, and what would you send or update?"
Review the AI's draft action and note what it got right and what it missed.
Share one step in your workflow where full AI autonomy would save the most time.

trends.title: AI Is Now Drafting Regulatory Filings — and Regulators Are Noticing
trends.body: The SEC published guidance this week acknowledging that AI-drafted regulatory disclosures are becoming common, and clarifying that companies remain fully responsible for AI-generated content in filings regardless of how it was produced. Meanwhile, several law firms reported that AI-drafted 10-K sections are now passing first-round review without material changes. One mid-size firm's general counsel estimated AI cut their annual disclosure preparation time by 40%, from six weeks to three and a half (Bloomberg Law, July 2026).

slants.strategy: When AI handles regulatory drafting at the quality level of experienced counsel, the competitive advantage goes to companies that can move faster through compliance cycles — streamline your regulatory calendar.
slants.operations: Compliance documentation, audit reports, and regulatory submissions are all prime candidates for AI-first drafting with human review — calculate the hours saved and reinvest them in higher-value compliance work.
slants.pm: Privacy policies, terms of service, and product compliance documentation are the PM's regulatory burden — AI-first drafting with legal review is the right workflow for teams without full-time legal support.
slants.admin: Board resolutions, compliance filings, and regulatory submissions that cross an executive admin's desk are increasingly AI-drafted documents — build your review skills for AI-generated regulatory content.

steps: Identify one document your organization produces that follows a standard regulatory or compliance format.

Open your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Help me draft a [document type] for a [type of organization]. Here are the key facts: [list the key inputs]. Follow standard format for this document type."
Review the AI's draft against the actual requirements and note what it got right and what needed correction.
Identify what information the AI needed that you had to provide versus what it supplied from its training.
Share how close the AI draft was to what you'd produce manually.

trends.title: AI Tutoring Is Closing Educational Gaps at Scale
trends.body: Khan Academy's AI tutor Khanmigo reported this week that students who used the tool for 30+ minutes per week over the past academic year showed 1.8 grade levels of reading improvement on average — with the largest gains in students who started below grade level. Schools in under-resourced districts saw comparable gains to schools with full-time tutoring programs, at roughly 2% of the cost per student (Khan Academy Research, July 2026). Educational AI is delivering the equity case its proponents promised.

slants.strategy: AI that delivers 1.8 grade levels of improvement in a school year signals that personalized, AI-powered learning at scale is not future-state — it's happening now. Build your L&D strategy around this capability.
slants.operations: The cost-efficiency of AI tutoring ($X per student vs. $50X for equivalent human tutoring) maps directly to corporate L&D: AI-powered skill development is dramatically more accessible than traditional training.
slants.pm: User onboarding and skill development for complex products can be AI-tutored — the Khan Academy model (personalized, adaptive, patient) is exactly what enterprise product training should look like.
slants.admin: AI tutoring that closes skill gaps at scale means the 'I never had training on this' barrier is lower than ever — use AI tutoring tools to build skills your formal training doesn't cover.

steps: Identify a skill gap in your work that you've been meaning to close but haven't had time to address through formal training.

Open your company-approved AI tool and ask it to tutor you on that skill: "I want to improve my understanding of [topic]. Act as a patient tutor. Start by asking me what I already know, then teach me the most important concepts at my level."
Engage for 15 minutes — answer its questions, ask follow-ups, and let it adapt to your level.
At the end, ask: "What's the one thing you'd suggest I practice this week to reinforce what we covered?"
Share the skill you worked on and one thing the AI taught you that surprised you.

homework.title: Build your AI skill gap list
homework.body: AI tutoring works best when you're specific about what you want to learn. This week, use AI to help you map your own skill gaps — then commit to closing one of them using AI-assisted learning.
homework.prompt: I want to identify the skill gaps most likely to limit my career growth in the next two years. Here's my current role and responsibilities: [describe]. Here are the AI tools I use regularly: [list]. Ask me five questions to understand my current skill level, then give me a ranked list of the five skills I should develop most urgently — and a learning plan for the top one.

2026-07-14.intro: Tuesday. Three things that matter right now — one about the economics of AI, one about how it's changing decision-making, and one about a new capability most people haven't noticed yet.

trends.title: AI Infrastructure Costs Are Falling Faster Than Expected
trends.body: Morgan Stanley's latest AI infrastructure report (July 2026) revised its cost projection models after surveying 200 enterprise AI deployments. The cost per AI-assisted task has fallen 78% in 18 months, driven by model efficiency improvements, chip advances, and competitive pricing pressure — and projections now show another 50% reduction over the next 12 months (Morgan Stanley Research, July 2026). The implication: AI workflows that aren't economically viable today will be table stakes within a year.

slants.strategy: When AI task costs fall 78% in 18 months, the ROI threshold for AI investment moves from 'significant ROI' to 'nearly everything passes' — revisit every AI use case you've shelved on cost grounds.
slants.operations: Operational AI at scale is now economically viable for workflows that weren't worth automating 12 months ago — run the math on every high-volume process your team owns.
slants.pm: AI feature costs in your product are falling fast — features that were too expensive to include in your roadmap should be reconsidered as the cost structure shifts beneath you.
slants.admin: Falling AI costs mean the productivity tools you use professionally will continue to improve and get cheaper, not more expensive — the habit-building you do now compounds on increasingly capable infrastructure.

steps: Identify one AI use case you've shelved because the cost, time, or effort wasn't worth it.

Open your company-approved AI tool and revisit it: "I want to reconsider whether this is now worth building or automating: [describe the use case]. What would this take to implement today, and what's the ROI if it saves [time/money estimate]?"
Do a rough ROI calculation based on the AI's assessment.
Decide whether it's worth bringing back to the roadmap.
Share one use case you're reconsidering and why the economics have shifted.

trends.title: AI Is Changing How Executives Make Decisions — Not Just How Fast
trends.body: Deloitte's AI in the C-Suite survey (July 2026) found that 71% of executives who regularly use AI for decision support report changing the quality of their decisions, not just the speed. The most commonly cited changes: considering more options before deciding, identifying blind spots earlier, and stress-testing assumptions more thoroughly. Only 12% of executives said they were using AI primarily for drafting and communication — 88% said AI's primary value was analytical (Deloitte, July 2026). The highest-value executives use AI to think better, not just work faster.

slants.strategy: The executives getting the most from AI are using it as an analytical partner, not a writing assistant — the highest-value prompt is 'challenge my thinking on this,' not 'write this for me.'
slants.operations: More thorough assumption-testing and earlier blind spot identification are exactly what operations leaders need for complex system decisions — build AI into your pre-decision review process, not just your post-decision documentation.
slants.pm: PMs who use AI to stress-test their roadmap assumptions and identify blind spots will make better prioritization decisions — make AI-assisted devil's advocate review part of your planning cycle.
slants.admin: Understanding how executives use AI most effectively helps you frame AI tools better when introducing or recommending them — lead with analytical value, not drafting efficiency.

steps: Think of a decision you're currently working through — a recommendation, a priority call, or a strategic choice.
Open your company-approved AI tool and lay out your current thinking.
Ask: "Challenge my thinking on this. What assumptions am I making that could be wrong? What options haven't I considered? What would a smart critic say about this approach?"
Engage genuinely with the pushback — don't just dismiss it.
Share one assumption the AI challenged that you're going to investigate before deciding.

trends.title: Real-Time AI Fact-Checking Is Coming to Every Screen
trends.body: Google's Project Astra — its real-time visual AI — expanded to Android devices globally this week, enabling AI to analyze what's on your screen and provide context, corrections, and related information without being asked. Meanwhile, OpenAI confirmed that a similar capability is in development for iOS. In early user testing, real-time screen AI identified factual errors in news articles, highlighted outdated statistics in presentations, and flagged biased framing in news summaries — in real time as users read (Google Labs, July 2026).

slants.strategy: Real-time AI fact-checking on every screen changes the standard for accuracy in communications — assume that anything your organization publishes will be AI-reviewed by sophisticated readers.
slants.operations: Operational reports, data dashboards, and status communications that go external should be stress-tested against AI fact-checking tools before distribution — errors are easier to catch before publishing.
slants.pm: Real-time screen AI that flags outdated statistics and biased framing in presentations means your stakeholder decks will face a higher accuracy bar — build a fact-check step into your final review process.
slants.admin: Real-time AI on screen means the context behind any document — a news article, a policy, a report — is now just an AI query away. Use this to brief executives faster and more accurately.

steps: Find a recent document, article, or presentation you've read or produced.

Paste a section into your company-approved AI tool and ask: "Fact-check this passage. Identify any claims that should be verified, statistics that could be outdated, and assumptions that might be worth questioning."
Note what the AI flagged and whether you agree with the flags.
Apply the same review to one of your own recent communications.
Share what the AI caught that you hadn't noticed.

homework.title: Use AI to stress-test your most important current project
homework.body: The executives in Deloitte's survey are using AI to challenge their assumptions, not just execute on them. This week, try applying the same approach to your most important current project — give AI the full picture and ask it to find the holes.
homework.prompt: I'm working on [describe the project, goal, or decision]. Here's my current plan: [describe it]. Please act as a rigorous critic. What are the three most significant risks I'm not adequately addressing? What assumptions in my plan are most likely to be wrong? What would I need to know or change to be more confident this will succeed?

2026-07-15.intro: Wednesday. Midweek. The AI landscape is moving on multiple fronts simultaneously — productivity tooling, regulatory frameworks, and a new category of model capability that changes what's possible for individual contributors. Here's what matters.

trends.title: Anthropic Releases Claude 4 Opus — The Strongest Reasoning Model Yet
trends.body: Anthropic launched Claude Opus 4 this week, its most capable model to date, with dramatically improved performance on multi-step reasoning, coding, and extended context tasks. Available via API and Claude.ai, the model introduces 'extended thinking' mode — a visible chain-of-reasoning that lets users see how the model is working through a problem before delivering an answer. On standard academic benchmarks, Opus 4 scores above GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro on 14 of 17 categories, with particularly large gains in scientific reasoning and document analysis (Anthropic, July 2026). The reasoning gap between frontier and commodity models is widening.

slants.strategy: The best AI model for complex strategy work just got significantly better — if your team is still using basic prompting for strategic analysis, the gap between what you're getting and what's possible has grown.
slants.operations: Extended thinking mode is particularly valuable for operations work — seeing the reasoning chain helps you validate whether the AI is approaching a complex process problem correctly before it gives you a recommendation.
slants.pm: More capable reasoning on multi-step product problems means PMs can now use AI for more sophisticated trade-off analysis, dependency mapping, and requirements synthesis — rebuild your AI workflow assumptions.
slants.admin: The most capable AI to date is now available in tools you already use — the opportunity to uplevel your AI-assisted work is highest right now, before the techniques you develop become standard practice.

steps: Identify your most complex current work challenge — something with multiple variables, competing constraints, and no obvious answer.
Open your company-approved AI tool and present the full challenge with all its context.
Ask: "Think through this step by step before responding. Walk me through your reasoning as you work toward an answer, then give me your recommendation with confidence level."
Evaluate whether the reasoning chain revealed assumptions or gaps you hadn't considered.
Share one place where seeing the AI's reasoning changed whether you trusted the output.

trends.title: EU AI Act Compliance Deadline Creates a Rush — and an Opportunity
trends.body: The EU AI Act's first major compliance tier took effect this week for high-risk AI systems, requiring documented risk assessments, human oversight mechanisms, and audit trails for AI used in employment, credit, and healthcare decisions. A survey of 400 European companies found that only 34% were fully compliant as of the deadline, while 58% were in progress and 8% reported no preparation at all (PwC European AI Act Survey, July 2026). US companies with EU operations or customers are racing to understand their exposure.

slants.strategy: EU AI Act compliance is now a procurement criterion for European customers — companies with documented AI governance frameworks have a competitive advantage in European markets.
slants.operations: AI systems used in employment decisions, performance review, or HR workflows fall under high-risk categories — audit your AI use cases against the EU AI Act risk classification framework now.
slants.pm: If your product uses AI for recommendations, scoring, or decisions that affect users, your EU market access may depend on your compliance posture — add an AI Act impact assessment to your next product planning cycle.
slants.admin: AI governance documentation — audit trails, risk assessments, oversight logs — is becoming a standard operational requirement. Building these records now is far easier than reconstructing them after the fact.

steps: List three AI tools or AI-assisted processes your organization uses that touch employees, customers, or partners.

For each, ask your company-approved AI tool: "Under the EU AI Act risk classification framework, is this use case likely to be considered high-risk, limited-risk, or minimal-risk? Explain the key criteria."
Identify which of your AI use cases would most benefit from formal documentation.
Draft a one-paragraph description of one AI use case — its purpose, inputs, outputs, and the human oversight step — as a starting point for an AI use case register.
Share one AI use case in your organization that you think deserves more formal oversight.

trends.title: AI Is Now Writing and Running Its Own Code in Production
trends.body: GitHub Copilot Workspace — the agentic coding environment that generates, tests, and iterates on code with minimal human input — is now available to all GitHub Enterprise customers. In the first two weeks of broader availability, users completed over 1 million automated coding tasks, ranging from bug fixes to feature implementations. The median task completion time for a well-specified coding request was 4 minutes — versus 2.3 hours for a human developer tackling a comparable task from scratch (GitHub, July 2026). Agentic coding is no longer a research project.

slants.strategy: When agentic coding reduces development time by 97% for well-specified tasks, the strategic advantage shifts to organizations that can specify what they want clearly — invest in product and requirements quality.
slants.operations: Internal tools, workflow automations, and data pipelines that previously required developer time are now accessible to non-technical ops leads who can clearly articulate requirements — start building your list.
slants.pm: PMs who write tight specifications get 97% faster development turnaround from AI coding tools — the return on investment in requirements quality has never been higher.
slants.admin: Agentic coding completing 4-minute tasks means small software requests (a custom report, a simple integration, a data transformation) are now viable for non-technical teams to commission — know what to ask for.

steps: Think of one small software tool, automation, or report your team would find useful but has never been built because it's not a development priority.
Write a clear specification: what the tool does, what inputs it needs, what the output should look like, and who uses it.

Open your company-approved AI tool and share the specification: "Help me refine this software specification so it's clear enough for an AI coding agent to implement without ambiguity: [paste your spec]"
Note what the AI added, clarified, or questioned in the specification.
Share the refined specification and estimate how much time a working version of this tool would save per week.

homework.title: Map your AI skill gap against the year ahead
homework.body: You're halfway through 2026. The AI landscape has moved significantly since January — new models, new capabilities, new workflows. This is a good moment to assess where you are and where you want to be by the end of the year.
homework.prompt: It's mid-July 2026. I want to assess my AI skill level and set a goal for December 2026. Here's how I currently use AI: [describe your current usage]. Here's my role: [describe your role]. Ask me five questions to understand my skill level, then give me: (1) an honest assessment of where I am relative to professionals in my field, (2) the three skills or habits that would most accelerate my development, and (3) a specific 90-day plan to get there.

2026-07-17.intro: Today's stories all point to the same shift: AI is maturing from a technology question into a management one — how you pay for it, how you feed it, and which human skills it makes more valuable, not less.

trends.title: The real AI budget question isn't the model, it's the cleanup
trends.body: A McKinsey report out today reframes how leaders should think about agent costs: <cite index="30-1">Agentic AI tasks can use nearly 1,000 times more tokens than conventional code reasoning or chat-based AI tasks, the report said, "Per-token pricing has stopped being a useful measure for what enterprises actually pay for gen AI."</cite> The bigger surprise is where the money actually goes: <cite index="30-9">about 60 per cent an agentic task's costs, in fact, are tied to refining answers</cite>, not generating them. As McKinsey put it, <cite index="30-5">the decision to scale an agent is increasingly becoming a complex and fast-changing economics decision, not a technical one</cite>.

slants.strategy: When you build the AI business case next quarter, budget for revision cycles and retries, not just a per-seat license fee.
slants.operations: Before approving a new agent workflow, ask how much of its cost sits in verification and rework — that's the number that actually predicts your bill.
slants.pm: Bake cost variance into your AI-enabled project plans, since the same task can price out differently depending on how many times the agent has to try again.
slants.admin: The more back-and-forth you do polishing an AI draft, the more it's actually costing behind the scenes — tighter first requests save real money.

steps: Pick one recurring task you already hand to an AI assistant, like a weekly status summary or a meeting recap.
Run it once with a single, specific request instead of your usual back-and-forth: "Draft this in its final, polished form in one attempt — don't wait for me to ask for revisions."
Compare that one-shot result to how many rounds of editing you'd normally do to get the same quality.
Notice which part of the task — the first draft or the endless tweaking — actually took the most effort. That's the expensive part, for you and for the AI.
Share in the group: which task got cheaper (and faster) when you asked for the finished version up front?

trends.title: Your AI pilots are ready to scale — your data isn't
trends.body: McKinsey's tech insights team flagged a quieter constraint behind all the agentic AI headlines: <cite index="4-1">As companies push their AI pilots to scale, data is emerging as a constraint. Leaders are prioritizing data readiness</cite> before adding more automation. Separate industry research backs this up — <cite index="16-18">nearly 60% of AI leaders say legacy integration is a primary adoption challenge when implementing advanced AI like agentic AI</cite>. Translation: the tool isn't the hard part anymore. Getting clean, connected information into it is.

slants.strategy: Add "data readiness" as its own line item in your AI roadmap — it now predicts scale-up success more than the model choice does.
slants.operations: Before rolling an AI pilot out wider, audit whether the systems feeding it are consistent, not just whether the pilot worked in a clean test environment.
slants.pm: Build a data-quality checkpoint into your AI project timeline; assume the integration work takes longer than the AI setup itself.
slants.admin: If an AI tool gives you a confusing or incomplete answer, the problem is often messy source data upstream, not the tool — flag it instead of just re-prompting.

steps: Pick one workflow where you already lean on an AI tool — a report, a dataset, a status doc.
Ask your company-approved AI tool: "List the top 3 places in this workflow where you had to guess, or where the information you received was inconsistent or incomplete."
Read the output and see if any of those gaps are things you already suspected but hadn't named.
Pick one gap and flag it to whoever owns that data or process — a five-minute heads-up now saves a bigger headache later.
Share in the group what surprised you most about where the messiness lives.

trends.title: AI is making junior jobs demand senior judgment
trends.body: PwC's newest global jobs analysis found a real divide opening up in how AI reshapes careers. <cite index="24-1">Analysis of US data shows AI-exposed entry-level roles are seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills such as judgement and leadership. These roles grew 35% since 2019, while other entry-level roles declined by 10%</cite>. As the report put it, <cite index="24-6,24-7">the traditional relationship between experience and expertise is changing. AI is removing some of the routine work that once acted as an apprenticeship, while increasing demand for judgement, leadership and adaptability much earlier in careers</cite>.

slants.strategy: Rethink your talent pipeline assumptions — the old model of "years in seat before judgment calls" is compressing fast, and your planning cycles should account for it.
slants.operations: Look for the operational tasks AI has already absorbed on your team, then build in earlier, structured chances for junior staff to practice the judgment calls that remain.
slants.pm: When staffing projects, weigh a junior team member's decision-making instincts as heavily as their tool proficiency — that's the skill AI isn't replacing.
slants.admin: The routine parts of your role that AI now handles free up time for the parts that actually build your reputation: judgment, discretion, and knowing what matters.

steps: Pick one task in your role that AI now does quickly for you — drafting, summarizing, formatting, scheduling.
Ask your company-approved AI tool: "Given that AI now handles this task quickly, what judgment or leadership skill becomes more valuable for me to strengthen next?"
Read the suggestion and think of one real moment this week where that skill would have mattered.
Write down one small way to practice that skill in the next two weeks.
Share in the group what skill came up — you might spot a pattern across the team.

homework.title: Let AI plan your next weekend getaway
homework.body: Pick a free tool — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity — and use it to plan a short trip or day out you've been meaning to take. This time, instead of giving it all the details up front, make it work for the answer.
homework.prompt: Try this: "I want to plan a weekend trip but haven't picked a destination. Before you suggest anything, ask me questions one at a time about my budget, interests, and how much driving or flying I'm willing to do. Then give me your top 3 ranked recommendations with a one-line reason for each." Notice how asking it to question you first — instead of dumping everything at once — gets you a sharper, more personal answer.

2026-07-18.intro: Today's drop is about where AI decisions actually get made: which workflows leadership funds, which tools employees quietly reach for anyway, and which skills your team needs to protect on purpose.

trends.title: Companies are done crowdsourcing AI pilots — and starting to pick winners
trends.body: PwC's 2026 predictions call out a pattern most large companies fell into: letting every team run its own AI experiment and hoping something sticks. <cite index="41-6">Crowdsourcing AI efforts can create impressive adoption numbers, but it seldom produces meaningful business outcomes.</cite> The shift now is toward a smaller, sharper approach where <cite index="41-1,41-2">senior leadership picks the spots for focused AI investments, looking for a few key workflows or business processes where payoffs from AI can be big</cite> (PwC, 2026).

slants.strategy: This is your job now — picking the two or three workflows worth a real AI bet, and building the business case for why the rest wait.
slants.operations: Expect fewer scattered pilots landing on your desk and more concentrated, well-resourced rollouts with a clear ROI target attached.
slants.pm: You'll likely run one deep AI project instead of five shallow ones — plan for more scrutiny and higher stakes on the project you do get.
slants.admin: The 'try whatever tool you like' era may be winding down as your org standardizes around a chosen few — get familiar with the frontrunners early.

steps: Open your company-approved AI tool.
Prompt it: "List the 3 recurring tasks on my team that eat the most time each week and have the clearest, most measurable outcome."
Pick the one that feels most winnable — not the flashiest, the most measurable.
Follow up with: "Write a 3-sentence pitch for why this task should be our team's one focused AI project this quarter."
Read the pitch, tighten anything that sounds off, and share it in the group.

trends.title: Employees trust their own AI judgment more than their company's rules
trends.body: A 2026 PagerDuty survey of 1,250 office professionals found <cite index="21-8">two-thirds (66%) of workers who have used AI say they did so even though they believed it was not permitted under company policy</cite>. Even more striking: <cite index="21-1">a majority of office professionals (72%) believe they understand how to use AI for their job better than the team responsible for managing AI at their company</cite> (PagerDuty, June 2026).

slants.strategy: If two-thirds of your workforce is quietly using unapproved tools, your AI budget conversations are missing a huge piece of real usage data.
slants.operations: The workflow shortcuts your team found using personal AI tools are free signal — they show exactly where the approved tools fall short.
slants.pm: If your project plans assume everyone sticks to sanctioned tools only, you may be underestimating both your team's real capacity and its real risk.
slants.admin: Whatever time you're quietly saving with a personal AI tool is worth surfacing to your manager or IT — better to name it than hide it.

steps: Jot down 2-3 AI tools you personally use for work tasks, whether officially approved or not.
Open your company-approved AI tool and prompt: "Here are tasks I do weekly: [list your tasks]. Which of these could I realistically move to an approved tool instead of a personal one?"
Read the suggestions honestly — don't dismiss them just because switching feels inconvenient.
Note one task where you'd still reach for another tool, and ask yourself if that's a real capability gap or just habit.
Share your honest answer in the group — this works best when people are candid, not defensive.

trends.title: Half of executives already see their teams' thinking skills slipping
trends.body: BCG's June 2026 research names a real organizational risk: <cite index="31-20">in a global study of 70 C-suite leaders and senior executives across multiple industries, we found that half are already observing de-skilling in their organizations, and more than 60% believe that de-skilling will pose a material threat within the next three to five years.</cite> One fix already in motion: <cite index="31-1">at CNIL, France's data protection authority, managers are responsible for assessing employees' ability to challenge AI outputs — not just to use them</cite>, making that judgment a visible, evaluated part of the job.

slants.strategy: Build skill-preservation checkpoints into your AI rollout plans now — the gap shows up later as a bad forecast nobody caught in time.
slants.operations: Map which of your processes now depend so heavily on AI that no one on the team could run them manually if the system went down.
slants.pm: Add a human-only checkpoint to at least one project phase per cycle so your team's judgment gets exercised, not just outsourced.
slants.admin: Keep practicing your own drafting and proofreading instincts on at least a few tasks a week — don't let AI polish become your only quality check.

steps: Pick one recurring task you now complete almost entirely with AI help.
Do it once this week without AI, and time yourself.
Open your company-approved AI tool and prompt: "Ask me questions before answering: help me spot 2 judgment calls in [describe the task] where I should double-check an AI's output before trusting it."
Compare your unaided attempt to the AI's usual output — note where your instincts were sharper or shakier than you expected.
Share one honest takeaway in the group.

homework.title: Plan a weekend getaway without doing all the legwork yourself
homework.body: Pick a place you've been meaning to visit and use ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity to help you plan it — but make the tool work for the details, not just hand you a generic list.
homework.prompt: Try this: "I want to plan a 2-day trip to [destination] on a budget of [amount]. Before you suggest anything, ask me questions about my travel style, food preferences, and pace so your plan actually fits me." Notice how the questions the AI asks change the quality of what it gives you back — that's the habit worth keeping for bigger prompts later.

2026-07-19.intro: Today's throughline: as agentic AI moves from pitch deck to production, the winners are the ones who can tell real capability from relabeled automation, spot where agents are quietly touching routine buying decisions, and close the training gap before confidence collapses.

trends.title: Not every 'AI agent' is actually an agent — Gartner says stop assuming otherwise
trends.body: Gartner is telling planning leaders to stop taking agentic AI pitches at face value. At its Supply Chain Symposium, the firm warned that hype and "agent washing" are creating real risks for organizations under pressure to deliver results, and separately estimates that of the thousands of vendors now claiming agentic AI capability, only about 130 are building genuinely autonomous systems (Gartner, May 2026).

slants.strategy: Before you greenlight budget for an 'agentic' platform, require the vendor to show what it does that scripted automation couldn't already do.
slants.operations: Run any pilot on your messiest, most unpredictable real cases — not the vendor's clean demo — to see if it's a true agent or automation in a costume.
slants.pm: Add a vendor-evaluation checkpoint to your intake process so 'agentic' claims get tested against project requirements, not just marketing language.
slants.admin: When you're helping schedule or scope a new tool demo, ask the presenter directly what happens when the system hits something it's never seen before.

steps: Pick one AI tool or 'agentic' feature your team currently uses or is evaluating.

Open your company-approved AI assistant and ask it: "I'm evaluating a tool marketed as an 'AI agent' for [type of task]. Give me 5 specific questions I should ask the vendor to tell whether this is genuinely autonomous versus repackaged automation."
Compare the answers against what you already know about the tool and flag any gaps.
Share your checklist in the group so teammates can reuse it before their next vendor call.

trends.title: AI agents are quietly starting to do your reordering, renewing, and invoice-paying
trends.body: Away from the consumer shopping headlines, enterprise-side agents are already handling real recurring work: enterprise-side agents (Microsoft Copilot, Salesforce Agentforce, custom internal agents) reorder office supplies, renew SaaS subscriptions, and pay invoices on behalf of a company. The consumer version of this is moving more cautiously — OpenAI recently paused its Instant Checkout feature, a signal that even the biggest players think the infrastructure and trust layers aren't fully ready yet.

slants.strategy: Get ahead of spend visibility now — if agents start making micro-purchasing decisions, your forecasting model needs a line item for it.
slants.operations: Audit your recurring purchase and renewal workflows to identify which ones are low-risk enough to delegate to an agent with human approval built in.
slants.pm: Treat a first agentic-procurement pilot like any other project: define scope, approval checkpoints, and a rollback plan before it touches real spend.
slants.admin: You're well-positioned to own this shift — start learning how approval workflows for agent-initiated purchases actually work, since someone will need to monitor them.

steps: List three recurring purchase or renewal tasks your team handles manually (software renewals, supply reorders, invoice approvals).

Ask your company-approved AI assistant: "Here are three recurring purchasing tasks on my team: [list them]. Which, if any, would be safe to delegate to an AI agent with human approval built in, and what guardrails should I put in place first?"
Pick the safest candidate and sketch what a one-step human approval checkpoint would look like.
Share your idea in the group chat.

trends.title: Companies are training their leaders on AI — and leaving everyone else to figure it out alone
trends.body: New research is putting a number on something a lot of people feel but rarely see measured: 78% of organizational decision-makers feel confident using AI at work, versus just 43% of the workers below them. The report also finds that 36% of employees report self-teaching as their primary route to AI skills, compared to just 23% who received any formal employer training (TrustedTech, July 2026).

slants.strategy: Build training investment into the AI roadmap itself, not as an afterthought — the confidence gap is a business risk, not just an HR issue.
slants.operations: Identify which frontline teams are navigating AI tools alone and pair them with structured guidance instead of assuming they'll self-teach.
slants.pm: Add an AI-literacy check-in to project kickoffs so every team member — not just the lead — has a baseline before the work starts.
slants.admin: If formal training hasn't reached you yet, don't wait — a short, structured self-practice routine can close a lot of that gap on your own timeline.

steps: Think of one AI skill you've picked up mostly on your own, with little or no formal training.

Ask your company-approved AI assistant: "Act as a mentor helping me get better at using AI at work. Ask me three questions about how I currently use AI tools, then give me a simple two-week practice plan to build one specific skill."
Try one of the suggested exercises today.
Share your two-week plan in the group and invite a teammate to try it alongside you.

homework.title: Let AI plan your next low-key weekend — but make it ask you first
homework.body: This one's just for you: pick a free tool (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or Perplexity) and use it to plan a small weekend trip or day trip, but with a twist — you're going to make it interview you before it gives any answers.
homework.prompt: "I want to plan a low-key weekend trip within driving distance. Before you suggest anything, ask me at least five questions about my budget, interests, and who's coming — then give me three ranked options with a one-line reason for each."
